prompt: Two apps send the same amount of data a day. One sends it in a single request, the other in sixty small ones. Which costs more battery, and why?

choices.text: The same: battery follows the bytes
choices.why: The bytes are the cheap part; waking the radio is the expensive one.

choices.text: The single one, because it keeps the radio busy longer
choices.why: A few seconds more of transfer is far less than sixty tails.

choices.text: The sixty: every one wakes the radio
choices.why: Right. Each wake has its tail; the cost of a request is mostly the cost of waking up for it.

choices.text: The sixty, because small requests use more processor
choices.why: The processor is rarely what empties a phone's battery.

prompt: For the typical 3G radio in Android's guide, at least how many seconds does one data transfer keep the radio drawing energy?
Why does the radio stay at full power for seconds after a transfer ends?

choices.text: Waking from standby is slow, so it lingers
choices.why: Right. More than two seconds to come up from standby, so it lingers.

choices.text: Because the app forgot to release a wake lock
choices.why: The tail is the radio's own behaviour, wake lock or not.

choices.text: To finish sending data the app queued
choices.why: The transfer is over; the radio is waiting, not sending.

choices.text: The operating system keeps it up for push messages
choices.why: Push does not need the radio at full power between messages.

prompt: A function acquires a wake lock, throws an error halfway, and never reaches its release. What does the user notice?

choices.text: The screen stays on
choices.why: A wake lock can keep the processor running with the screen off.

choices.text: The app crashes on its next launch
choices.why: A held wake lock does not crash anything; it drains.

choices.text: A notification saying the app is running
choices.why: That is a foreground service; a wake lock shows nothing.

choices.text: A battery that drains with the screen off
choices.why: Right. The processor never sleeps, and nothing on screen says why.

prompt: Match each drain to the habit that wastes it.

pairs.right: kept awake after the user stopped looking

right_distractors: a large file sent once on Wi-Fi

prompt: When does an Android phone enter Doze?

choices.text: Whenever the battery falls below 20%
choices.why: Doze is about being left alone, not the battery level.

choices.text: Unplugged, still, screen off for a while
choices.why: Right. Moving it, the screen or a charger ends it.

choices.text: When an app has been in the background for a minute
choices.why: Doze is a state of the device, not of one app.

choices.text: Only at night
choices.why: Doze does not read the clock; it reads how the phone is lying.

prompt: During Doze, what happens to an app's network requests and ordinary alarms?

choices.text: They run at once, more slowly
choices.why: Network access is suspended, not slowed.

choices.text: They wait for a maintenance window
choices.why: Right. The system opens a short window now and then, and runs the deferred work in it.

choices.text: They are cancelled for good
choices.why: They are deferred, not cancelled.

choices.text: They run when the app opens a wake lock
choices.why: Doze ignores wake locks.

prompt: Put Android's App Standby Buckets in order, from fewest restrictions to most.
From Android 13, what puts an app in the restricted bucket, unless it is exempt?

choices.text: Asking for location in the background
choices.why: That is a permission question, not a bucket rule.

choices.text: Being installed from a file instead of a store
choices.why: The bucket follows use, not where the app came from.

choices.text: Holding a foreground service for an hour
choices.why: A foreground service is allowed; it is visible to the user.

choices.text: Going 8 days without the user opening it
choices.why: Right. It was 45 days on Android 12; Android 13 cut it to 8.

prompt: Which of these does a foreground service on Android 14 need? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A notification the user can see
choices.why: Right. Running in plain view is the point.

choices.text: A declared type, such as location or media playback
choices.why: Right. Without a type the system throws an exception at start.

choices.text: The permission that goes with that type
choices.why: Right. Each type has its own permission.

choices.text: A periodic interval of at least 15 minutes
choices.why: That is WorkManager's periodic work, a different mechanism.

prompt: An iOS app schedules a refresh with earliestBeginDate set to 07:00. At what time will it run?

choices.text: Not before 07:00
choices.why: Right. The system does not guarantee the date, only that it will not start earlier.

choices.text: At 07:00, if the app is in the foreground
choices.why: A background task is not tied to the app being open.

choices.text: Before 07:00, so that it is ready in time
choices.why: It will not begin sooner; that is the one promise.

choices.text: At 07:00, give or take a minute
choices.why: The date is a lower bound, not an appointment.

prompt: On Android, the shortest repeat interval periodic work accepts is ___ minutes.
Why is the planner's daily sync a batched job and not a timer?

choices.text: It has to run at exactly 08:00
choices.why: None of the three mechanisms can promise an exact time.

choices.text: A timer is not allowed in Kotlin
choices.why: The language allows it; the system would not honour it in the background.

choices.text: Nobody waits for it
choices.why: Right. A few hours late costs nothing, so it can wait for Wi-Fi and the charger.

choices.text: The server accepts one request a day
choices.why: The server is not the reason; the battery is.

prompt: In the iOS version, why does the handler call scheduleSync() before it starts the sync?

choices.text: iOS has no periodic request
choices.why: Right. Each run asks for the next one first, so a run cut short still leaves one waiting.

choices.text: Because iOS runs tasks in the order they were submitted
choices.why: Order is not the point; there is no periodic request at all.

choices.text: To make the sync start sooner
choices.why: earliestBeginDate is a day away; nothing starts sooner.

choices.text: It is required before setTaskCompleted
choices.why: No such rule; the order is a choice for safety.

prompt: Match each platform's way of saying 'only when it is cheap'.

pairs.right: battery and network, decided by the library

prompt: What does Result.retry() do in the WorkManager worker?

choices.text: Runs doWork again at once, in a loop
choices.why: WorkManager waits before trying again.

choices.text: Cancels the periodic job
choices.why: That would be giving up; retry keeps it.

choices.text: Tries later, with a backoff
choices.why: Right. The same idea lesson 14 wrote by hand, done by the system.

choices.text: Shows the user a Try again button
choices.why: A background job has no screen.

prompt: A team wants the planner to remind a student at 18:45 that a session starts at 19:00, and plans a background task for 18:45. What is wrong with the plan?

choices.text: Nothing, if the phone is charging
choices.why: Even on the charger, the system chooses the moment.

choices.text: A reminder at a set time is a notification
choices.why: Right. A scheduled local notification is the tool for a moment; lesson 17.

choices.text: Background tasks cannot read the clock
choices.why: They can read it; they cannot choose when they run.

choices.text: The task should be periodic, every 15 minutes
choices.why: Every 15 minutes at most, and still at the system's choice.

prompt: Polling every minute, how many times a day does the model wake the radio?
Why does batch.ts call itself a model rather than a measurement?

choices.text: Because Node.js cannot run on a phone
choices.why: That is true and beside the point: no device was measured at all.

choices.text: Its output has been rounded
choices.why: Rounding is not what separates a model from a measurement.

choices.text: Its numbers are random
choices.why: It prints the same numbers on every run.

choices.text: No radio was measured
choices.why: Right. Every number traces to a constant and its source.

prompt: On a 5G network the radio's tails are different. Which of the model's results still holds?

choices.text: That polling every minute keeps the radio awake 432 minutes
choices.why: The minutes come from the 3G tails and change with them.

choices.text: That one batched job costs 0.2 minutes
choices.why: That number is the 3G tail too.

choices.text: The ratio, about 1,440 to one
choices.why: Right. Each wake-up costs the same, so the ratio is the count of wake-ups.

choices.text: None: with other tails nothing carries over
choices.why: The ratio carries over, as long as the polls do not overlap.

prompt: Polling every 10 seconds, the model says the radio is awake all 1,440 minutes of the day. Why not 8,640 × 18 seconds?

choices.text: The next wake-up comes before the tail ends, so seconds would be counted twice
choices.why: Right. Math.min counts each second of the day once.

choices.text: Android refuses requests closer than 10 seconds apart
choices.why: No such rule; the overlap is arithmetic.

choices.text: The model rounds to whole days
choices.why: It prints minutes with one decimal.

choices.text: Low power does not count as awake
choices.why: The awake column counts every power above standby.

prompt: Using the model's assumptions, how many seconds is one wake-up worth at full power, counting the low-power tail at half?
A news app polls its server every minute in a foreground service, so that headlines are always fresh. What does this lesson suggest instead?

choices.text: Poll every 15 minutes with WorkManager instead
choices.why: Better than every minute, and still 96 wake-ups for nothing new.

choices.text: Poll every 10 seconds so each request is smaller
choices.why: Smaller requests do not help; wake-ups are the cost.

choices.text: Keep polling, and hold a wake lock so it is reliable
choices.why: That adds a second drain to the first.

choices.text: Let the server push when there is news, and batch the rest
choices.why: Right. Being told replaces asking, and the rest waits for a cheap moment.

prompt: Which statements hold on both Android and iOS? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Deferred work runs when the system decides
choices.why: Right. Both treat background work as a request.

choices.text: Work can be limited to a charging phone
choices.why: Right. setRequiresCharging and requiresExternalPower.

choices.text: Periodic work runs every 15 minutes exactly
choices.why: 15 minutes is Android's minimum, not a promise, and iOS has no periodic request.

choices.text: Apps are ranked into standby buckets
choices.why: Standby buckets are Android's.
